lines.en: Molly MacCormack was Irish.
Massive reveal, I know. But seeing as it’s relevant to today’s scenario, I figured I’d just remind you now and get it out of the way.
Anyway, with the groundwork in place and a baseline level of understanding hopefully established, we come now to the setting of our next injection of Decorated Melancholy.
It’s a new designer drug that has just hit the streets and is now making everyone joyously depressed, as contradictory as that may seem to you suburban folk.
Here are two addicts now — two girls obsessed with the highs and lows that come from the manifestations of tonal whiplash, but each for their own reasons. And each with their own goals.
Today, however, those goals aligned. And they fully intended to strip and cosplay and touch each other in the privacy of a fitting room. Just two of those were truths and one was a lie.
It’s easy to lie about the future, though. Or things you cannot see. Which is one more reason we need to acknowledge the Irish elephant in the room.
Because no matter how badly she wanted it, and no matter how deeply she felt it, Molly MacCormack would always be lying when she told herself she belonged here.
And all it took to let everyone else know was a single glance.
: Are you sure this place is going to have lingerie? It seems kind of tame at first glance.
: Aye. There’s a section behind that curtain over there with more risque costumes.
: We just need to wait for the right opportunity to enter since we’re still in high school and they don’t want us to be horny yet.
: That’s actually really unfair when you realize that this is probably the horniest segment of our lives.
: Good point. Excuse me! Can we-
: Wow! Nihongo jouzu desu ne!
: Uh...thank you. But I was about to ask if-
: Where are you from?
: Ireland. Can my friend and I go look through the 18+ section, please?
: Excuse me, can you tell your Irish friend that section is for adults only?
: Wait, are you talking to me? Why? She’s speaking in perfect Japanese.
: It’s just easier for you to understand. I don’t want to confuse her.
: She’s fluent, though.
: I actually live here.
: Wow! Nihongo jouzu desu ne! For school? How long are you staying?
: Forever. Though, it’s not like there’s much of an option to begin with at the moment.
: Forever? Sugoi. Why are you studying Japanese? Do you like anime?
: Yes. But-
: Excuse me, can you ask your Irish friend how long she’s staying? It’s not really “forever,” is it? Did she use the wrong word, maybe?
: What part of “she’s fluent and she lives here” do you not understand?
: Is she half-Japanese? Or is she just here to visit you?
: Are you even listening?! She-
: It’s fine, Ami. You don’t need to get worked up on my behalf.
: But-
: This is just what happens as a foreigner sometimes. You just have to deal with it.
: Woooow! Nihongo jouzu desu ne...
: This lady might be overdoing it a little, though.
: A little is being almost too nice when, if anything, your Japanese is even better than mine.
: Can you ask her if I can take a picture? We don’t get many foreign customers here.
: Yeah, just let me spend a few years of my life studying even half as hard as she does so I can say it to her in English like you apparently want me to.
: Oh, you don’t know English? Then how do you two communicate?
: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHHHHHHH!!!!!! SCREW YOU, LADY! WE’RE GOING TO GET DRESSED UP LIKE SEXY CATS NOW AND THERE’S NOTHING YOU CAN DO TO STOP US!
: Hah...we probably should have just entered the 18+ section without asking.
Molly MacCormack was Irish. And she was constantly reminded of that.
But despite the pride she had of her own heritage, it didn’t shake the feeling that it was used almost mockingly at times. Like a tool or a label to separate her from her surroundings.
And while she’d made a name for herself around these parts in particular as someone who really did live here, there would always be people like this one who simply didn’t understand that.
It was merely a way of life for her.
But the true burden is that this is how it’s always been. And that she never felt truly at home where she was born either. Which is one more reason she lives in her own world.
No one can make her feel like she doesn’t belong there.
: Oisín, what’s the hold-up?! We’re not eating in the classroom, are we? People are going to think we’re like them if we don’t have lunch in the cafeteria.
: But I brought lunch from home today and everyone always tries to take it when we go there.
: Probably because your idea of “lunch” is four bags of Tayto and leftover fifteens. You need to eat better! You need to-
: What’d you bring for lunch, Molly?
: Huh? What? I didn’t-
: I asked what you brought for lunch. It looks...exotic.
: Oh! Yes, I suppose it is. They call it a “bento” in Japanese. It’s a boxed lunch with a variety of different-
: Is there, like...raw fish in there then? Sushi is Japanese, right? Or is that Chinese?
: It’s Japanese. They eat other stuff too, though. For example, I learned to make something called “Inarizushi” last night, which is actually deep fried tofu-skin called “aburaage” and-
: Woah, you cook? I figured you just played games and watched Japanese cartoons all day.
: I try sometimes if there’s something my dad can’t make. I think it came out okay, though. Do you want some? I’m not really hungry right now.
: Oh, uh...me either. I already ate and I don’t like raw stuff anyway.
: Okay. But if you change your mind-
: Wait, are you reading porn right now?
: Huh? No. That’s just how they draw the-
: Aoife, look. That’s totally porn, isn’t it?
: Hm? I...aah! What are you showing me?! Why’s Molly bringing cartoon porn into school again?! Didn’t she already get in trouble for that once?!
: It’s just a regular manga! And besides, the porn you’re talking about is called “hentai.” At least get the name right if you’re going to accuse me of something.
: Oh my god, she would know how to say it in Japanese.
: You actually watch that stuff, Molly? Do you not like regular people or something?
: Of course she doesn’t like regular people. Colin had a crush on her and she just ignored him because some new game came out.
: The backpack kid? With the weird metal headband who’s always rushing everywhere?
: Yeah, they’re perfect for each other. I think his dad died too so their parents could get together as well.
: Too far, Aoife. Too far.
: What do you mean? I like Molly. She’s just weird, but in a cute way. Like I want to help her be normal and stuff.
: What’s wrong with being weird? I don’t mind being an outcast if I get to do what I like.
: So you’re just happy not having any friends?
: I have friends online. We’re grinding heroics after school today to gear up a new recruit.
: Translation — I don’t have any friends. Come on, Orla. Let’s go to the cafeteria and let the weeaboo read her Japanese cartoon porn without us getting in the way.
: Do you want us to bring you back anything, Molly? Like, actual food?
: No thank you. I’ll be okay.
: If you insist. Would you mind spotting me a few pounds, though?
: Didn’t I just give you money yesterday?
: Did you? I don’t remember. Either way, your dad is loaded, isn’t he? I just need enough to buy lunch.
: I haven’t borrowed money in a while, Molly. You can lend it to me and I can let Orla use it. See how good of a friend I am?
: Uh...I guess you can look in my bag if you really need it.
: Ew, I’m not gonna find anything weird in there, am I? Because if I see tentacle porn again, I’m telling the teacher.
: Maybe I should just go through it then.
Molly MacCormack knew she was being bullied, but never felt the need to do anything about it since it was mostly inoffensive jabs at her interests and five-pound loans that would never be repaid.
So long as she could maintain the life she had at home, she’d be “happy.” But happiness here was quiet. And despite how “happy” she was to be alone, that loneliness still burnt at times.
Particularly on days like this, where she’d open the doors to an empty home and her voice would echo upon calling out-
: Tadaima...
As if her father would even know what that meant if he were here to greet her.
So she’d retire to her room, where she spent the vast majority of her life up to this point, and enter one more world where it felt like she belonged.
Where loans were repaid, death was only temporary, and anyone you didn’t want to come into contact with could be blocked with the press of a button.
That urge to cut people off was a lot less rampant here, however, for these people were like her.
: Stop standing in fire, you fucking morons. Do the world a favor, uninstall the game, and go back to Toontown Online if you’re going to play like a literal child.
It still existed, though, because some people were just really bad at online games and it wound up dragging everyone else down by mere association.
: What do you mean you have projected textures off?! No wonder you’re standing in shit then! Just turn them on! Are you running the game off a fucking potato?! Do better!
: Molly? Can I come in?
: Healer bio! Dad aggro!
: Door’s open!
: Are ya winning, son?
: Dad, what did I tell you about acting out that meme every time you come in?
: One day, you are going to laugh. How was school?
: Normal. Everyone is still an NPC.
: Even me?
: No, you’re a side character. It’s different.
: Is that a new staff?
: You don’t need to pretend to know what you’re looking at, Dad. Are you making dinner tonight or are we ordering again?
: If we’re going to order, it needs to be now. I have some business in Belfast in a few hours and probably need to spend the night there.
: Bring back yellowman from Aunt Sandra’s, please. Will you be back tomorrow?
: Early. Can I trust you to not keep yourself awake on energy drinks all night? Because you’re grounded if I come home and you’re still up.
: Grounding me is a good thing. All it does is remove the pressure I have to leave the house and be the outgoing, social butterfly you wish me to be.
: And if I take your computer away?
: You wouldn’t...
: Bed by midnight. Understood?
: Aye. But I’m not happy about it.
: Then how about I make it up to you by letting you choose where we get dinner from? I heard there’s a new ramen shop nearby.
: Ramen’s never good delivered. All it will do is make me wish for the real thing.
: You’ve never had the real thing. We’ve never left Ireland and, according to you, all of the Japanese restaurants here are run by Chinese people who are just-
: Capitalizing on the trendiness on Japanese food, aye.
: But mark my words...One day, I will get to experience the real thing. And live out my days as a real Japanese high-schooler and the true heroine of someone’s life.
: You’ll always be my heroine, Molly. No matter where the wind takes you.
: I’m sorry, Dad. But I’m hoping for a route with a lot less consanguinity and a lot more catgirls.
: Yet, somehow, I have ended up with both.
: I’m sorry you had to experience all of that racism out there, nyaa. Would it make you feel better if I let you pet me for a little while?
: So it fits, after all. I was worried it wouldn’t given your bust size or lack thereof.
: Hisssssssss!
: You look very cute, Ami. I truly hope it helps instill whatever sexual feelings you hope to implant in your father.

: Why don’t you put yours on? Because, despite what that employee lady might have led you to believe, sexy catgirls are not specific to Japanese culture. You shouldn’t feel ashamed to partake as well, nyaa.
: I have never felt shame for even a moment in my life. You have no idea what you are saying.
: Well, that’s good. Because I was seriously about to scratch that lady’s eyes out if she Nihongo-jouzu’ed you one more time. You’re just as Japanese as me as far as I’m concerned.
: I appreciate that. But you don’t need to lie, Ami.
: Nyaa?
: I’m not Japanese. I’m Irish. And I’m glad to be Irish. Even if my specific brand of Irishness is still hotly contested by a group of belligerent extremists.
: I know nothing about Ireland but, if that makes you happy, that’s fine by me. I just don’t want you feeling left out.
: I can assure you I still feel more welcome here than I ever did at home. And that’s even with the thousands of times I’ve been Nihongo-jouzu’ed.
: Woooooow. Nihongo jouzu desu ne.
: I will lock you in a cage for good.
: I’d probably be better off in there.
